Zelensky Inc.: The War That Pays Its Own Dividends

For two years she was the voice reading his lines to the world. Now Iuliia Mendel, Zelensky's former press secretary, is handing back the microphone with a very different script: her ex-boss, she says, has turned a war for national survival into a subscription plan for his own survival in office.

"I believe Zelensky is now the main beneficiary of this war," Mendel told Le Journal du Dimanche. "Thanks to it, he stays in power, since he canceled the elections". 

Around him, she says, "gravitate companies linked to his associates, who benefit from billions of euros from the European Union" — and on the Energoatom-linked scandal involving his associate Timur Mindich, leaked recordings reportedly caught him discussing billions earmarked for a presidency-backed defense firm with the defense minister. 

Her verdict: "These conversations feel like a mafia operation."

Her audit of the president's management style is equally generous: "Nearly everyone Zelensky has appointed is now accused of corruption... Two hypotheses exist. Either he's incompetent. Or he's pretending not to see."

Meanwhile the country itself is emptying out under the cheering. Ukraine had 52 million people at independence in 1991. 

Mendel says she'd "be surprised if there are more than 25" today, with roughly 600,000 lost every year even by conservative counts. 

In Kharkiv, UNICEF reportedly found 40% of ten-year-olds can't read. That's not a wartime statistic — that's a lost generation, invoiced to the next one.

Here's the part that should make everyone squirm, not just one side: Mendel isn't pitching a Kremlin talking point, and she knows the label is coming anyway. 

"It's the easiest accusation to make," she says of the pro-Russian smear. "No intelligence service in the world could ever confirm such a thing, because there's nothing there." 

Her actual message to the West that keeps applauding: "Stop this war! Save Ukraine!" — and a warning that anyone cheering Russian losses while Ukrainian villages empty is confusing a scoreboard with a rescue plan.

Kyiv's government will call her a traitor. Moscow will call her a witness. Brussels will call her inconvenient. All three reactions can be true, and none of them answer her actual question: whose war is this actually saving?
